findings.paper_title: Annual Plan and Budget 2026-27 addendum final
findings.headline: Council tax increased to maximum allowable level with social care precept
findings.detail: Essex County Council's council tax element increased by 3.95% for 2026/27, combining 1.95% general increase with 2% adult social care precept, resulting in Band D charge of £1,641.96. This uses both the general increase power and the dedicated social care precept, hitting the referendum threshold and leaving no room for future increases without public approval.
findings.matters: Council tax increases at the referendum cap indicate financial pressure and limited future flexibility for revenue-raising. This matters alongside the structural budget gap, as the council has exhausted its principal flexible revenue source.
findings.figures: 3.95% total increase (1.95% general + 2.00% adult social care); Band D £1,641.96; Total precept requirement £936.8m
findings.quote: That Essex County Council's element of the council tax be increased by 3.95% comprising of a 1.95% increase in general council tax and 2.00% adult social care precept.

findings.paper_title: Annual Plan and Budget 2026-27 addendum final
findings.headline: Structural budget gap persists despite improved government settlement
findings.detail: The final government funding settlement increased by £3.982m and non-domestic rates by £782,000, allowing Essex to reduce planned reserve drawdowns significantly. However, the council still requires £1.841m from the Everyone's Essex Reserve to balance the 2026/27 budget, down from the originally planned £6.411m. This indicates an underlying structural gap between ongoing spending and revenues from council tax and grants.
findings.matters: Lenders assess whether a council's budget is structurally balanced from normal revenues or requires annual reserve draws. Persistent draws indicate structural imbalance and raise questions about medium-term financial sustainability as reserves deplete.
findings.figures: Reserve draw reduced from £6.411m to £1.841m; Government funding increase £3.982m; NNDR increase £782,000
findings.quote: This reduces the draw on reserves to balance the 2026/27 budget to £1.841m.

findings.paper_title: Everyone’s Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 – Part 2: Budget and Plan
findings.headline: Operational restructuring required to achieve budgeted efficiency savings
findings.detail: The council states that staffing reorganisation and operational reshaping will be required in some areas to deliver efficiency gains assumed in the budget. Specific staffing implications will be addressed under implementation plans but are not detailed in this report.
findings.matters: Restructuring carries delivery risk. If implementation is delayed or costs more than budgeted, it could create mid-year funding shortfalls. Service disruption during transition could also affect income from fee-paying services.
findings.figures: Not quantified; part of broader efficiency requirement embedded in £1,432.5m budget
findings.quote: An element of reorganisation and reshaping will be required to support efficiency gains in some operational areas.

findings.paper_title: Everyone’s Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 – Part 2: Budget and Plan
findings.headline: Council tax raised to the maximum permitted level, with social care precept at ceiling
findings.detail: Essex is increasing council tax by 3.95% (1.95% general + 2.00% adult social care precept). The 2% adult social care precept is at the maximum allowed. The 3.95% total sits below the anticipated 5% referendum threshold, but exhausts the social care precept and leaves minimal headroom for further increases.
findings.matters: The council has removed a key lever for responding to future pressures. The social care precept cannot be raised further. If settlement is worse than assumed or social care costs exceed budget, the only option would be unplanned savings or service cuts.
findings.figures: 3.95% increase (1.95% general + 2.00% social care precept); 5% referendum threshold; Band D rises from £1,579.59 to £1,641.96
findings.quote: Essex County Council's element of the council tax be increased by 3.95% comprising of a 1.95% increase in general council tax and 2.00% adult social care precept.

findings.paper_title: Everyone’s Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 – Part 2: Budget and Plan
findings.headline: Budget finalised without confirmed government settlement; NNDR returns still being processed
findings.detail: Final settlement detail had not been received when the budget report was published; receipt expected on or after 9 February 2026. Final NNDR returns from districts remain outstanding, with impacts being worked through due to substantial changes from the Fair Funding Review. An addendum report will be issued once these are confirmed.
findings.matters: The £1,398.8m budget is provisional. Both settlement funding and business rates income—key components of the £1,432.5m budget—are not yet confirmed. Adverse settlement or NNDR outcomes could require mid-year rebalancing and threaten budget deliverability.
findings.figures: £936.8m from council tax (of £1,398.8m net requirement); NNDR element unconfirmed
findings.quote: Detail of the final settlement had not been received at the time the Council agenda was required to be published. We anticipate that this will be received on or after 9 February 2026. The final NNDR returns are still being worked through by Districts, which reflects the substantial changes to Business Rates as part of the Fair Funding Review.

findings.paper_title: Everyone’s Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 – Part 2: Budget and Plan
findings.headline: Adult social care charging savings reduced after Cabinet meeting; £306k rebalancing required
findings.detail: The day opportunities charging saving was reduced by £306,000 and offset by increased savings from the Live at Home contract. This rebalancing during budget finalization indicates planned savings are proving harder to deliver. Adult social care comprises 66% of gross council spending and was subject to significant budget adjustment.
findings.matters: The council's largest and most pressured spending area is showing implementation difficulty. Savings that were initially planned are proving unachievable, signalling broader vulnerability to cost pressures in social care. This is material for lenders assessing budget robustness.
findings.figures: £306,000 reduction; 66% of £1,432.5m budget on health and social care
findings.quote: This has resulted in a £306,000 reduction in the saving delivered through charging for day opportunities, offset by a corresponding increase to the Live at Home contract saving.

findings.paper_title: 05 AGS Cttee Dec 2025 - Auditors Annual Report - 2024-25 - Appendix
findings.headline: Pension Fund investments understated by £41.44 million; auditors lack full assurance over asset valuations
findings.detail: The Pension Fund auditor identified a £41.44 million understatement in investment values. The Council obtained an updated actuarial report indicating this particular understatement does not impact the reported pension liability (since liability is actuarially determined, not asset-based). However, the valuation misstatement indicates broader gaps in asset assurance on the balance sheet.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are the council's largest obligation. Valuation errors in supporting assets undermine confidence in the liability position and indicate unresolved audit gaps on material balance sheet items.
findings.figures: £41.44 million understatement in pension fund investments; separate finding of £34.9 million understatement in Level 3 investments (Pension Fund)
findings.quote: We received our assurance letter from the Pension Fund auditor. They identified an understatement of £41.44 million in the value of investments reported in the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: 05 AGS Cttee Dec 2025 - Auditors Annual Report - 2024-25 - Appendix
findings.headline: Schools' High Needs Block deficit growing from £11.6 million to £243 million by 2028/29
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block closed 2024/25 with an £11.6 million deficit and is forecast to grow to £243 million by 2028/29. This is a cumulative statutory liability the council cannot escape; it grows each year and represents unsustainable provision for special educational needs and related costs.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is a hidden liability outside the council's control (it depends on pupil needs, not council policy). A £243 million obligation by 2028/29 is material and will constrain the council's ability to fund other services or invest—it may require government intervention or claw-back.
findings.figures: Closing deficit £11.6 million (2024/25); forecast to grow to £243 million by 2028/29
findings.quote: High Needs Block (Dedicated Schools Grant): Deficit closing balance of £11.6 million, this is forecast to grow to £243 million by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: 05 AGS Cttee Dec 2025 - Auditors Annual Report - 2024-25 - Appendix
findings.headline: Children's and Adults Social Care overspent by £21.2 million in 2024/25, driven by sustained demand pressures
findings.detail: The two largest service areas overspent by £21.2 million despite savings targets. Overspend was driven by rising demand and higher costs for care packages and placements, particularly complex cases. This is structural—linked to demographic trends and cost inflation in a demand-led service. The overall council surplus was achieved by lower borrowing costs and higher investment returns, masking the underlying deficit.
findings.matters: Social care is the council's largest spending area and a statutory demand-led service. Persistent overspends are structural, recur annually, and signal either uncontrollable demand or failed cost management—both material credit risks.
findings.figures: £21.2 million overspend in 2024/25; social care demand described as 'persistent and growing'; additional inflation costs £4.7 million above budget
findings.quote: Children's and Adults Social Care overspent by £21.2 million, driven by complex care needs and demand pressures.

findings.paper_title: 05 AGS Cttee Dec 2025 - Auditors Annual Report - 2024-25 - Appendix
findings.headline: Budget gap of £129 million by 2028/29 despite delivery of savings plans
findings.detail: The council forecasts a structural budget gap growing from £26 million in 2026/27 to £129 million by 2028/29. Inflation accounts for £111 million; cost pressures (social care demand, capital, changing demographics) add £48 million. Planned savings of £104 million through 2028/29 would reduce this to £25 million—still unresolved.
findings.matters: This signals the council cannot fund its current service model from available resources, even with aggressive savings. If savings delivery slips or demand exceeds forecast, the gap grows dramatically; it implies future service cuts or significant additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Gap £26m (2026/27) rising to £129m (2028/29); inflation £111m; new burdens £48m; planned savings £104m; residual gap £25m
findings.quote: The financial strategy forecasts a budget gap of £26 million in 2026/27 rising to £129 million in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: 05 AGS Cttee Dec 2025 - Auditors Annual Report - 2024-25 - Appendix
findings.headline: Auditors cannot confirm 2024/25 financial statements are accurate; disclaimer of opinion issued
findings.detail: The auditors did not obtain sufficient evidence over financial statement balances and movements to issue a standard unqualified opinion. They cannot verify property valuations or opening balances carried forward from 2023/24 (when a disclaimer was also issued). This is part of a multi-year programme to rebuild assurance.
findings.matters: A lender's assessment depends on reliable financial statements. A disclaimer of opinion means the council's actual financial position cannot be verified; asset valuations, reserves, and liability positions remain unconfirmed.
findings.figures: Lack of assurance over Property, Plant and Equipment and Investment Property valuations; opening balances from 2023/24 also unassured
findings.quote: Although the level of assurance gained has increased, we have not yet obtained sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Heavy reliance on reserve drawdowns to bridge gap; net £4.934m drawn down in 2025/26 and key reserves being consolidated
findings.detail: The council drew down £35.762m from earmarked reserves in 2025/26 and transferred only £30.828m back in, a net draw of £4.934m. Beyond this, it is moving £17.804m between reserves, notably to create two new reserves (County Priority Reserve and Community Innovation and Improvement Fund Reserve) by consolidating and redirecting funds from Commercial Investment, Ambition Fund, Everyone's Essex, Renewal Fund, and Equalities Fund reserves. This reallocation suggests reserves are being prioritised for strategic/discretionary projects rather than held for financial resilience. The report notes reserves are 'necessary to ensure the Council's continued financial resilience to future financial challenges and known pressures,' yet the pattern is depletion.
findings.matters: Lenders track reserve adequacy as a buffer against volatility. A net £4.934m drawdown plus £17.8m reallocation signals reserves are tight relative to identified risks (DSG, social care demand, inflation). The closing General Balance is sufficient to fund only 17 days of operating expenditure.
findings.figures: £35.762m drawn from reserves; £30.828m transferred to reserves; net £4.934m drawn down; £17.804m reallocation between reserves; General Balance covers 17 days operating expenditure
findings.quote: Approval is sought for £4.934m (net) to be transferred from earmarked reserves. This comprises of £35.762m drawn down from reserves and £30.828m transferred into reserves.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Revenue underspend of 0.4% masks dependency on one-off interest rate windfall; medium-term outlook is 'incredibly challenging'
findings.detail: The small 0.4% revenue underspend (£5.050m) is described as a positive outcome, but is entirely dependent on transient factors: £10.5m external interest receivable due to higher cash balances and elevated rates; £4.2m underspend on borrowing costs from early repayment of long-dated loans. The council explicitly warns these are 'only one-off' factors and notes 'the risk now highlighted is that we continue to see demand pressures due to pent up demand filtering through.' The medium-term outlook is characterised as 'incredibly challenging' with 'ongoing demand pressures and market volatility in social care,' 'significant pressure on the High Needs Block,' 'projected increases in unemployment,' and 'highly probable' continued volatility in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assume the 0.4% underspend baseline repeats. The council is signalling that 2026/27 will be tighter, with interest rates likely to normalise and demand pressures unabated. The narrow margin offers little resilience.
findings.figures: 0.4% revenue underspend (£5.050m on £1.199bn budget); £10.5m interest receivable; £4.2m borrowing cost underspend; both flagged as one-off
findings.quote: However, the risk now highlighted is that we continue to see demand pressures due to pent up demand filtering through (over and above the significant growth that has been allowed for in the 2026/27 budget), while some of the factors that have contributed to the under spend in 2025/26 are only one-off (e.g. interest receivable).

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered at only 71% of original budget; £4.7m in abortive costs funded from reserves
findings.detail: Original capital budget was £367.109m; delivered £260.422m. This is 82% of the final approved budget (£316.480m) but only 71% of original. The underspend (£56.059m) includes £4.7m in abortive costs on Army & Navy, Fairglen, and M11 Junction 8 schemes. The council cites delays from Homes England on Housing Infrastructure grant extensions and 'use of unused contingency on alternative projects, which is not anticipated to be a repeated issue in future years.' This last phrase signals the underspend is not sustainable—contingency was pulled forward and won't be available next year. The council also warns of 'significant cost escalation' risks ahead from inflation and market supplies.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the 29% underspend on original budget is structural (capacity to deliver capital) or cyclical (timing and contingency use). The council signals it is cyclical and expects higher delivery rates in 2026/27. Abortive costs of £4.7m represent capital deployed without outcome.
findings.figures: Original budget £367.109m; final approved £316.480m; delivered £260.422m (71% of original; 82% of final); £56.059m underspend; £4.7m abortive costs (Army & Navy, Fairglen, M11 J8)
findings.quote: This is mainly due to the delay in Homes England confirming extensions to the Housing Infrastructure grant funding deadlines, which is now reflected in this position, and the use of unused contingency on alternative projects, which is not anticipated to be a repeated issue in future years.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: External auditor has issued two consecutive disclaimed opinions; clean opinion for 2025/26 is uncertain
findings.detail: Ernst & Young, the council's auditor since 2023/24, disclaimed an opinion on 2023/24 accounts, reporting insufficient resources to undertake the required work. In 2024/25, EY completed a full audit but issued a disclaimed opinion because they could not gain assurance over opening balances brought forward from 2023/24. For 2025/26, EY plan to rebuild audit assurance over prior-year balances, 'but it is unclear at this stage whether they will be able to undertake sufficient work to be able to issue a clean audit opinion on the Council's accounts in 2025/25.' This is a governance weakness running for two financial years with no clear resolution in sight.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on audited accounts if the auditor is unable to give a clean opinion. Two consecutive disclaimers combined with uncertainty about 2025/26 suggest either audit capacity or financial record-keeping weaknesses that are not being resolved.
findings.figures: Two consecutive disclaimed opinions: 2023/24 and 2024/25; 2025/26 opinion uncertain
findings.quote: EY did not undertake an audit of the 2023/24 financial statements owing to EY reporting that they had insufficient resources to undertake the required work. They therefore issued a disclaimed opinion in order to close the audit by the statutory backstop date of 28 February 2025. Although EY did complete a full audit for 2024/25, they did not undertake any work to be able to gain assurance over the opening balances for the year which were brought forward from 2023/24. Consequently, EY issued a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 Accounts as well. EY plan to undertake work, as part of the 2025/26 audit, to rebuild audit assurance over balances brought forward from prior years, but it is unclear at this stage whether they will be able to undertake sufficient work to be able to issue a clean audit opinion on the Council's accounts in 2025/25.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Children's services placements driven £6.8m overspend after drawing down over £14m of reserves, with structural capacity shortfall
findings.detail: Children's Services overspend £6.797m after mitigating with £14m+ of reserve drawdowns (£7.785m from Children's Risk Reserve, £1.982m from Children's Sustainability Reserve, £4.028m from Early Intervention reserve). The paper attributes this to external mainstream residential at 139 placements vs budget of 103 (£11.342m overspend alone), 28 high-cost unregistered arrangements (£5.512m), and external fostering placements at higher volumes than recruitment can supply. The underlying issue is pent-up demand and complexity—these are not one-off variances but structural. The report notes that 'pent up demand filtering through (over and above the significant growth that has been allowed for in the 2026/27 budget)' continues.
findings.matters: A lender sees a service that cannot fit demand into budget even with £14m of reserve mitigation. The budget already included 'significant growth' for 2026/27, yet the report expects further pent-up demand. Reserves available for this purpose are finite.
findings.figures: £6.797m overspend after £14m+ reserve drawdown; 139 external mainstream placements vs 103 budgeted; 28 unregistered placements; £11.342m from external residential alone; £4.418m from external fostering
findings.quote: Children's Services which has an over spend of £6.797m after using over £14m of reserves to offset pressures driven by demand, price and complexity of need.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit will hit £33.6m by end of 2025/26 with no permanent funding solution after 2028
findings.detail: The DSG high needs block carries forward a £24.494m overspend in 2025/26. The accumulated deficit reaches £33.6m. The statutory override that permits carrying this forward expires 31 March 2028; after that, the full deficit must be financed from general fund and usable reserves unless further government action materialises. A new High Needs Stability Grant will cover 90% of the accumulated deficit up to end 2025/26, but this is pending Department for Education approval of a local SEND reform plan. The council has set aside £31.3m in DSG General Risk reserve as mitigation. This is described as 'one of the largest issues the organisation currently faces'.
findings.matters: A lender faces repayment risk if a £33.6m deficit must be absorbed into general reserves within three years, or if the stability grant is not approved. This is a hard deadline with no discretionary mitigation.
findings.figures: £33.6m accumulated deficit; £24.494m 2025/26 overspend; 90% covered by stability grant pending DfE approval; statutory override expires 1 April 2028; £31.3m set aside in DSG risk reserve
findings.quote: The statutory override that permits this only exists up to 31 March 2028 - on 1 April the statutory override falls away and, unless further changes are made, the accumulated deficit will be returned to the General Fund, and must be financed from the grant and/or the Council's usable reserves.

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: High dependency on government grant funding (26% of gross spend) with falling real value
findings.detail: £514m of the council's funding comes from specific and general grants (26% of gross expenditure excluding DSG). Government has stated grant uplifts will be below inflation from 2027/28 onwards, while statutory service demands (social care, SEND) continue to rise, creating a squeeze.
findings.matters: As the largest single funding source after local taxes, grants provide limited flexibility. Below-inflation uplifts on a base already declining relative to need means the council will find it increasingly difficult to fund statutory services, forcing either reserve depletion or service rationing.
findings.figures: £514m grant funding; 26% of gross expenditure (excluding DSG); uplifts below inflation from 2027/28
findings.quote: ECC has become increasingly reliant on Government grant funding in recent years to offset rising demand pressures for our services. The 2026/27 revenue budget is funded by £514m of specific and general Government grants, which is 26% of gross expenditure (excluding Dedicated Schools Grant).

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: Business rates reform creating risk to collection and local business viability
findings.detail: The 2026 business rates revaluation combined with removal of RHL relief (from 40% to 14%) creates a significant jump in rates bills for leisure, hospitality and retail businesses. This compounds existing pressures from National Insurance rises and high interest rates, risking business closures and rateable value reductions.
findings.matters: A collapse in business rates collection would directly reduce council income. This is a real risk given the stated concern in the paper about businesses' ability to afford rates. Loss of business rates base is harder to recover than council tax.
findings.figures: RHL relief reduction from 40% to c14%; revaluation reset to baseline (removing accumulated growth); safety net reduces from 100% to 92.5% by 2028/29
findings.quote: the new RHL multipliers are 5p less than the normal small and standard multipliers, which represents a c14% reduction in rates paid. Compared to the 40% RHL reliefs given to local businesses in 2025/26... this represents a comparably sizeable increase in rates paid by local businesses in this sector

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: Capital borrowing costs escalating from 8.6% to 11.9% of net budget by 2029/30
findings.detail: The council plans £392m of borrowing over the next four years to fund capital investment. The revenue cost of servicing this debt will rise from 8.6% of the £1.4bn net budget in 2026/27 to 11.9% by 2029/30, consuming an additional £0.5bn+ in annual revenue servicing costs.
findings.matters: Escalating debt service consumes scarce revenue resources at a time when spending pressures are rising. This locks the council into fixed obligations that crowd out discretionary spending, reducing flexibility when deficits hit £110m+ in outer years.
findings.figures: £392m planned borrowing over 4 years; 8.6% of net budget in 2026/27; 11.9% by 2029/30; £104m (27%) from return-on-investment schemes
findings.quote: The revenue costs of borrowing to finance the capital programme will rise from 8.6% of the net budget in 2026/27, to 11.9% by 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: Unrestricted reserves declining 34% by 2029/30; general reserve covers only 17 days of operations
findings.detail: Unrestricted reserves will fall from current levels to £209m by 2029/30 (a 34% reduction). The general balance of £68m is now only 5% of net budget and covers just 17 days of operations, below the historical 6% target and inadequate for a council of this size facing high volatility.
findings.matters: Reserves depletion combined with structural deficits means the council has limited financial shock absorption. A single major demand spike or income shortfall in 2027/28 when the gap hits £110m could force emergency borrowing or service cuts.
findings.figures: £316m current unrestricted reserves declining to £209m (£107m reduction); £68m general reserve; 5% of budget; 17 days coverage
findings.quote: By 2029/30 it is anticipated that the balance of unrestricted reserves will have reduced to £209m (a reduction of £107m or 34%)

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: Savings delivery carrying 37% medium-to-high delivery risk
findings.detail: Of £41m savings assumed in the 2026/27 budget, only 63% (£25.7m) have high confidence. 37% (£15m) carry medium or high delivery risk, including the unproven Placements Strategy and technology-led efficiencies that may not materialise on schedule.
findings.matters: Reliance on high-risk savings to close budget gaps means the council is exposed to slippage. If even half the at-risk savings fail, the council will need further reserve draws or in-year cuts. This is a structural vulnerability.
findings.figures: £41m total savings; £25.7m (63%) high confidence; £6.5m (16%) medium risk; £8.5m (21%) high delivery risk
findings.quote: At this stage, 63% (£25.7m) have a high level of confidence, with 16% (£6.5m) medium risk and 21% (£8.5m) of savings having a high level of delivery risk.

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: Government grant funding declining despite sector growth; Essex losing out to formula redistribution
findings.detail: Essex will receive £7.5m less grant funding in 2026/27 than 2025/26, and a further £6m reduction by 2029/30, despite total local government funding growing nationally. The government's Fair Funding Review redistributes money away from rural/shire councils to urban and metropolitan areas.
findings.matters: A council losing grant share whilst facing rising demand (especially social care) faces a structural funding disadvantage that cannot be resolved through council tax alone. The proxy council tax rate formula penalises low-tax councils like Essex.
findings.figures: £7.5m less grant 2026/27 vs 2025/26; £6m further reduction by 2028/29; £514m specific and general grants (26% of gross expenditure)
findings.quote: ECC will be in receipt of £7.5m less grant funding for 2026/27 compared to 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: Children's placements facing £10.3m overspend in 2025/26 with no permanent solution
findings.detail: Despite in-year savings delivery across the council, children's placements are overrunning by £10.3m in 2025/26 due to rising complexity and insufficient market capacity. The 2026/27 budget assumes £34m growth in children's services (16%) with reliance on unproven placement strategy savings.
findings.matters: An uncontrolled overspend in the current year signals demand forecasting weakness and raises the risk that 2026/27 children's services budget assumptions will similarly prove insufficient. Placements spending is typically inelastic—difficult to cut quickly.
findings.figures: £10.3m 2025/26 overspend; £34m (16%) growth assumption 2026/27; £49m demographic pressure including £34m for children's placements
findings.quote: unprecedented budget pressures are being experienced across children's placements and the Council is currently forecasting a £10.3m over spend in 2025/26 despite in-year savings being on track for delivery in total

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: High Needs Block deficit accelerating to £102.8m in 2026/27 despite new funding
findings.detail: The SEND/High Needs Block deficit will grow from current levels to £102.8m in 2026/27, then to £178.8m by 2027/28. While a statutory override allows the council to defer this technically, it creates real cash pressure that accelerates the need for external borrowing.
findings.matters: This is a £102.8m quasi-liability growing annually with no clear funding solution until 2028/29. It forces the council to either borrow or exhaust cash balances, increasing leverage and debt service costs. It represents an unfunded mandate.
findings.figures: £102.8m deficit forecast 2026/27; £178.8m by 2027/28; £89.6m after 1% Schools Block transfer
findings.quote: While the statutory override has been extended to 2027/28, we are still waiting for further guidance on how these deficits will be managed, and how proposed changes to funding from 2028/29 will work in practice.

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget requires £6.4m reserve draw to balance
findings.detail: The only year shown as 'balanced' in the MTRS is 2026/27, and only after drawing £6.4m from the Everyone's Essex reserve. This immediately signals structural imbalance and indicates reserves are being used to mask an operating deficit.
findings.matters: Use of reserves to balance annual budgets rather than addressing structural spending is a red flag for lenders. It depletes buffers and signals the organisation is not living within its means, reducing financial resilience.
findings.figures: £6.4m reserve draw; £1,432m net expenditure budget
findings.quote: the 2026/27 budget is not balanced without drawing on £6.4m of reserves

findings.paper_title: Everyone's Essex Annual Plan and Budget 2026/27 - Part 1: Section 151 Officer's Report
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit doubling to £279m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The S151 Officer reports the forecast budget gap will reach £279m by 2029/30, more than double the prior year forecast. With a £110m gap for 2027/28, this represents a rapidly deteriorating medium-term position that requires urgent delivery of major savings programmes.
findings.matters: A £279m structural gap across an £1.4bn net budget signals the council will struggle to balance without severe spending cuts, asset sales, or further borrowing. The trajectory threatens financial sustainability and serviceable debt levels.
findings.figures: £279m gap by 2029/30 (up from £110m implied previously); £110m gap 2027/28; £1.4bn net expenditure budget 2026/27
findings.quote: We currently forecast the budget gap by the end of the MTRS in 2029/30 will be £279m, which is over double the size of the gap faced in the final year of the MTRS at this point last year.

findings.paper_title: 3.Appendix 2024-25 Audit Results Report for ECC
findings.headline: Audit procedures remain incomplete at report date; final opinion subject to change pending outstanding work.
findings.detail: At the date of the audit results report (13 November 2025), multiple audit procedures were still outstanding, including completion of testing on material group transactions, S106 grants, transactional income and expenditure, and senior audit team review. The auditor explicitly states 'the audit process is still ongoing' and that 'the final disclosures in the financial statements which could influence our final audit opinion' remain subject to challenge.
findings.matters: Incomplete audit procedures at this stage of the financial year indicate potential preparedness issues. The possibility that 'the final audit opinion' could still be influenced by outstanding work suggests material uncertainties may yet emerge before the audit is concluded.
findings.figures: Not quantified; affects completeness of audit evidence for all areas under review
findings.quote: Given that the audit process is still ongoing, we will continue to challenge the remaining evidence provided and the final disclosures in the financial statements which could influence our final audit opinion, a current draft of which is included in Section 04.

findings.paper_title: 3.Appendix 2024-25 Audit Results Report for ECC
findings.headline: Five PFI schemes represent £76.4 million current liability and £219.5 million in committed future payments over 15 years.
findings.detail: Essex County Council operates five Private Finance Initiative schemes (A130 Bypass, Debden Park School, Clacton Secondary Schools, Castleview/Cornelius Vermuyden/Columbus Schools, and Woodlands School). The schemes currently carry a £76.4 million liability on the balance sheet and commit the council to £219.5 million in operational payments over the next 15 years, before accounting for inflation or availability deductions.
findings.matters: PFI payments are a committed fixed obligation on the council's revenue budget and reduce financial flexibility. The scale of future commitments (£219.5 million) is material to assessing the council's capacity for additional borrowing or service changes.
findings.figures: £76.417 million current PFI liability; £219.507 million in future payments over 15 years
findings.quote: There is a liability outstanding to pay the PFI contractors for capital expenditure of £76.417 million as at 31 March 2025. Payments remaining to be made by the Council under the operational phase of its PFI contracts (excluding any estimation of inflation and availability / performance deductions) total £219.507 million over the next 15 years.

findings.paper_title: 3.Appendix 2024-25 Audit Results Report for ECC
findings.headline: Pension Fund auditor identified £41.44 million understatement in investment values, though council's liability impact assessed as immaterial.
findings.detail: The auditor for Essex Pension Fund identified a £41.44 million understatement in the value of investments reported in the pension fund financial statements, with Essex County Council's share being £12.87 million. Essex obtained an updated IAS19 actuarial report from the pension fund actuary which concluded this would not impact the council's recorded pension liability. However, the fact that an error of this magnitude was found in pension fund accounting merits monitoring.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are material to councils' balance sheets and borrowing capacity assessments. Large errors in pension accounting, even if ultimately determined not to impact this council's recorded liability, indicate wider audit quality issues in the pension fund administration.
findings.figures: £41.44 million understatement in pension fund investments; £12.87 million attributable to Essex County Council
findings.quote: They have identified an understatement of £41.44 million in the value of investments reported in the financial statements. The Council has obtained an updated IAS19 report from the Actuary, which shows this would not impact the Council's Pension Liability.

findings.paper_title: 3.Appendix 2024-25 Audit Results Report for ECC
findings.headline: £1.791 billion property and investment property portfolio cannot be fully assured due to cyclical revaluation program.
findings.detail: Essex County Council revalues only 20% of its property and investment property portfolio each year on a rolling 5-year cycle. In 2024/25, only £422.8 million out of £1.791 billion (23%) was revalued. The auditor explicitly states they are 'unable to obtain full assurance over the completeness and valuation of Property, Plant and Equipment and Investment Property at 31 March 2025' and is awaiting specialist reports before drawing conclusions.
findings.matters: A material portion of the council's balance sheet cannot be independently verified. Property represents the largest asset class for local authorities, and valuation uncertainty creates risk for lenders assessing collateral and net worth.
findings.figures: £1.791 billion total PPE balance; £422.8 million revalued in 2024/25 (23%)
findings.quote: The Council deploys a cyclical valuation process, securing valuations for 20% of its portfolio each year. As a consequence it is not possible to gain assurance over the whole PPE and IP portfolio valuation at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: 3.Appendix 2024-25 Audit Results Report for ECC
findings.headline: Disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements due to continuation of prior-year audit restrictions.
findings.detail: The auditor has issued a disclaimer of opinion on Essex County Council's financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025. This follows a disclaimer of opinion in 2023/24, which prevented completion of the detailed audit procedures required to build sufficient assurance. The auditor explicitly states they were unable to complete procedures necessary for an unmodified audit opinion. The disclaimer affects the entire financial position reported by the council.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the external auditor cannot provide any assurance over the accuracy of the financial statements. This is the highest-level audit concern and indicates significant governance/capacity constraints in the council's financial accounting and audit process.
findings.figures: Not quantified, but affects all material balances in the 2024/25 financial statements
findings.quote: we have not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion on these financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Essex Pension Fund Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Pension fund moving to negative cashflow from 2026-27, requiring investment income realisation to meet benefit payments
findings.detail: The Essex Pension Fund is currently cash-positive (£1m net in 2025/26) but is forecast to move into increasingly large deficits: £13m in 2026/27, £15m in 2027/28, and £30m in 2028/29. To bridge the gap between contribution income and benefit expenditure, the fund will realise income from its UK property portfolio through Border to Coast Pension Partnership. The fund holds £217.2m in custodian cash to support this transition.
findings.matters: Essex County Council as administering authority will face rising pension fund deficits, requiring increased employer contributions and creating ongoing pressure on council revenue budgets. Lenders need to account for this future obligation when assessing the council's financial capacity.
findings.figures: Net cashflow excl. investment income: 2024/25 actual 13, 2025/26 estimate 1, 2026/27 forecast (13), 2027/28 forecast (15), 2028/29 forecast (30). Custodian cash holdings at 31 Dec 2025: £217.2m total (Sterling £152.2m, Dollar £55.9m, Euro £8.4m).
findings.quote: The Fund is maturing, and analysis has been undertaken to forecast when new contributions (employees and employers including deficit) are not enough to meet all benefit payments falling due... The current position is that the Fund is broadly cash positive for 2024/25 & 2025/26, and forecasts negative cash balances for the years 2026/27 to 2028/29.

news_drafts.lead: Council tax increases at the referendum cap indicate financial pressure and limited future flexibility for revenue-raising. This matters alongside the structural budget gap, as the council has exhausted its principal flexible revenue source.

news_drafts.lead: Lenders assess whether a council's budget is structurally balanced from normal revenues or requires annual reserve draws. Persistent draws indicate structural imbalance and raise questions about medium-term financial sustainability as reserves deplete.
